questions.q: What does the reparameterisation trick write a sample from $\mathcal N(\mu, \sigma^2)$ as?
questions.why: Randomness moves into ε, which doesn't depend on the parameters, so gradients flow through μ and σ.

questions.q: What is the KL divergence $KL(\mathcal N(\mu, \sigma^2) \,\|\, \mathcal N(0, 1))$ for one dimension?
questions.why: It is zero only when μ = 0 and σ = 1. For a diagonal Gaussian, sum this over dimensions.

questions.q: What is the score of a distribution?
options: The gradient of its log density with respect to the data, $\nabla_x \log p(x)$
Its derivative with respect to parameters
questions.why: The score points toward higher density and doesn't depend on the normalising constant, which is why it is easy to model.

questions.q: What is the score of $\mathcal N(\mu, \sigma^2 I)$ at x?
questions.why: Differentiate $-\|x - \mu\|^2/(2\sigma^2)$. The score points back toward the mean, more strongly for smaller σ.

questions.q: For a Gaussian mixture, how is the score at x formed?
options: The score of the nearest component only
The sum of all component scores with equal weight
A posterior-weighted average of each component's score
The score of the mixture mean
questions.why: $\nabla \log p = \sum_k r_k(x)\,\nabla \log \mathcal N_k(x)$ with responsibilities $r_k$ computed by a softmax over log weighted densities.

questions.q: Why compute Gaussian mixture responsibilities in log space?
options: It makes the weights sum to more than one
Densities far from a component underflow to zero; log-sum-exp keeps them stable
questions.why: In high dimensions every density can underflow, giving 0/0. Working with log densities avoids that.

questions.q: Adding independent Gaussian noise $\mathcal N(0, \sigma_2^2)$ to $x \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma_1^2)$ gives what distribution?
questions.why: Variances of independent Gaussians add. This is why many forward steps collapse into one closed-form jump.

questions.q: Why is the KL divergence between two Gaussians useful in diffusion training?
options: It removes the need for noise
The variational bound splits into KL terms between Gaussian posteriors and model steps, each with a closed form
questions.why: With fixed variances, each KL reduces to a weighted squared error between means, which leads to the noise-prediction loss.

questions.q: In DDPM, what is $\bar\alpha_t$?
options: The sum of the β values
The noise level at step t only
questions.why: It is the fraction of signal variance left at step t. It falls from near 1 to near 0.

questions.q: What is the closed-form forward sample $x_t$ given $x_0$?
questions.why: Training can jump straight to any t without simulating the chain.

questions.q: What was the motivation for the cosine noise schedule?
options: It removes the need for β
The linear schedule destroys information too quickly at low resolution, wasting many late steps on near-pure noise
questions.why: Cosine defines $\bar\alpha_t$ directly so it decreases more gradually in the middle, and clips β to avoid a singularity at the end.

questions.q: What is the signal-to-noise ratio at step t?
questions.why: The schedule's whole effect can be described by how log-SNR changes over t.

questions.q: What does "zero terminal SNR" mean?
options: At the last step $\bar\alpha_T = 0$ exactly, so $x_T$ is pure noise with no leftover signal
The SNR is zero at the first step
questions.why: Common schedules leave a little signal at T. Training then sees slightly informative noise that sampling never matches, which limits very bright or dark images.

questions.q: When rescaling a schedule to zero terminal SNR, which prediction target is recommended and why?
options: v-prediction, because at $\bar\alpha_T = 0$ predicting ε from pure noise gives no information about $x_0$
questions.why: When $x_T = \epsilon$, an ε-predictor can output its input and learn nothing. v-prediction still asks for $x_0$ at that step.

questions.q: In a linear β schedule from 1e-4 to 0.02 over 1000 steps, what is $\bar\alpha_{1000}$ roughly?
questions.why: The sum of β is about 10, so $\bar\alpha_T \approx e^{-10}$. That is small but not zero, which is the issue zero-terminal-SNR rescaling fixes.

questions.q: Why is the forward process chosen to be fixed rather than learned in DDPM?
options: So $x_t$ can be sampled in closed form and the training target is simple
questions.why: The model only has to learn the reverse. Some later variants learn the schedule, at extra complexity.

questions.q: How is the timestep t given to the denoising network?
options: As a sinusoidal embedding passed through an MLP and added or used to modulate features in each block
As an extra image channel filled with t
As a one-hot vector concatenated to the output
It isn't; the network infers it
questions.why: Sinusoids give smooth, multi-frequency features of t, much like positional encodings in transformers.

questions.q: In a time-conditioned residual block, a common way to inject the time embedding is what?
options: Multiply the input image by t
Project it to per-channel scale and shift (or a bias) applied after a normalisation layer
Concatenate it to the output only
Replace the skip connection with it
questions.why: Scale-and-shift conditioning (like FiLM or AdaGN) lets each channel's behaviour depend on the noise level.

questions.q: Why does a U-Net suit denoising?
options: It works only at one resolution
Skip connections pass fine detail from the encoder to the decoder while the bottleneck sees global context
questions.why: The output must match the input resolution exactly, and noise must be removed at every scale.

questions.q: Where in the U-Net is self-attention usually added?
options: At the lower-resolution levels, where the number of positions is small enough for attention to be affordable
questions.why: At 64×64 there are 4096 positions; at 16×16 only 256, which makes the quadratic cost manageable.

questions.q: In a spatial self-attention block, what are the tokens?
options: The spatial positions of the feature map, each a C-dimensional vector
questions.why: The H×W×C map is flattened to (HW) tokens of size C, attended over, then reshaped back, usually with a residual connection.

questions.q: Why is group normalisation preferred over batch normalisation in diffusion U-Nets?
options: It is the only normalisation that works with convolutions
It doesn't depend on batch statistics, which vary with small batches and mixed noise levels
questions.why: Each batch mixes very different timesteps, so batch statistics would blend unrelated inputs.

questions.q: What does the network output in standard DDPM training?
options: A tensor of the same shape as the input image, such as the predicted noise
questions.why: Whatever the target (ε, $x_0$ or v), it has the shape of $x_t$.

questions.q: Why do output layers in diffusion models often start at zero initialisation?
options: So each residual block starts as identity and training begins from a stable point
questions.why: Zero-initialised final convolutions are a common stabiliser in deep residual generators.

questions.q: What is the simplified DDPM training loss?
options: $\|\epsilon - \epsilon_\theta(x_t, t)\|^2$ with t uniform and $x_t$ built from $x_0$ and ε
The negative log-likelihood of $x_0$ under a Gaussian
questions.why: It drops the per-timestep weights of the variational bound and works better in practice for sample quality.

questions.q: What is the mean of the forward posterior $q(x_{t-1} \mid x_t, x_0)$?
options: A weighted combination of $x_0$ and $x_t$ with coefficients from the schedule
questions.why: $\tilde\mu = \frac{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\beta_t}{1-\bar\alpha_t}x_0 + \frac{\sqrt{\alpha_t}(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})}{1-\bar\alpha_t}x_t$. The reverse model plugs in its estimate of $x_0$.

questions.q: What is the posterior variance $\tilde\beta_t$?
questions.why: It is slightly smaller than $\beta_t$. DDPM found both choices for the reverse variance work similarly.

questions.q: Given a predicted ε, how do you recover the predicted $x_0$?
questions.why: This inverts the forward formula. It is noisy at large t because it divides by a small $\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}$.

questions.q: What is v-prediction?
options: Predicting the next image in a video
Predicting the velocity of the sampler only at t = 0
questions.why: v stays well-scaled at all noise levels and gives both $x_0$ and ε by simple linear combinations with $x_t$.

questions.q: What does Min-SNR loss weighting do?
options: Caps each timestep's weight at min(SNR, γ) (adjusted for the target), so low-noise steps don't dominate training
Weights every step equally in $x_0$ space
Sets weights to the SNR exactly
questions.why: Different timesteps compete for model capacity. Clamping their weights speeds convergence.

questions.q: Why does ε-prediction implicitly weight timesteps differently in terms of $x_0$ error?
options: It emphasises only the last step
It doesn't; the weighting is uniform
The ε loss equals the $x_0$ loss times the SNR, so it emphasises low-noise steps
questions.why: The $\hat x_0$ error is the ε error divided by $\sqrt{\text{SNR}}$, so the squared ε error equals SNR times the squared $x_0$ error.

questions.q: Why is t sampled uniformly during training rather than going through steps in order?
options: Each step's loss is an independent regression problem, and uniform sampling covers all of them without simulating chains
Uniform sampling makes the loss zero
The model only sees one step per epoch
questions.why: Some methods sample t non-uniformly, or by log-SNR, to focus on harder noise levels.

questions.q: What does one DDPM ancestral step do?
options: Runs the forward process once more
Subtracts the predicted noise and stops
Computes the posterior mean from the predicted noise and adds fresh Gaussian noise scaled by the step's standard deviation
questions.why: $x_{t-1} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}(x_t - \frac{\beta_t}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}}\hat\epsilon) + \sigma_t z$, with no noise added at the last step.

questions.q: How does classifier-free guidance combine predictions?
options: It uses only the unconditional prediction
It averages conditional and unconditional predictions
questions.why: w > 1 pushes samples toward the condition. The same network learns both by dropping the condition for some training examples.

questions.q: What is the main trade-off as the guidance scale increases?
options: Better prompt adherence and sharper images, but less diversity and eventually oversaturated artifacts
questions.why: Very high w moves samples off the data manifold, which shows up as harsh colours and repeated textures.

questions.q: What does DDIM with η = 0 give?
options: A stochastic sampler identical to DDPM
A sampler that only works for 1000 steps
A deterministic sampler that maps each noise sample to one image and can skip many steps
questions.why: DDIM reuses the DDPM-trained model. η interpolates between deterministic (0) and DDPM-like (1).

questions.q: In one DDIM step from t to s, what quantities are used?
options: The predicted $\hat x_0$ and $\hat\epsilon$, recombined at noise level s
questions.why: $x_s = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_s}\hat x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_s}\hat\epsilon$ when η = 0.

questions.q: Karras-style samplers parameterise noise by σ. How is $x$ written?
options: $x = x_0 + \sigma\epsilon$, with σ decreasing from σ_max toward 0
questions.why: This "variance exploding" view turns sampling into solving an ODE in σ. An Euler step uses $dx/d\sigma = (x - \hat x_0)/\sigma$.

questions.q: Why do Karras schedules space σ values more densely near zero?
options: Because the model is untrained at high noise
Errors at low noise levels affect fine detail most, so smaller steps there improve quality for the same number of steps
To make sampling faster at high noise
questions.why: The schedule interpolates $\sigma^{1/\rho}$ linearly with ρ = 7, concentrating steps at small σ.

questions.q: Why is noise not added at the final DDPM step?
options: It is added, but scaled by 1000
Noise can't be added to images
The output should be the clean sample; adding noise at t = 1 would only blur it
questions.why: The last step returns the posterior mean (or $\hat x_0$).

questions.q: What does denoising score matching train the network to predict?
options: The score of the noised data distribution, using $-\epsilon/\sigma$ as the target
questions.why: For $\tilde x = x + \sigma\epsilon$, the score of $q(\tilde x | x)$ is $-\epsilon/\sigma$. Minimising the squared error recovers $\nabla \log q_\sigma(\tilde x)$.

questions.q: How is ε-prediction related to the score?
options: The score is ε times the SNR
questions.why: A noise predictor is a scaled score model, which links DDPM to score-based models.

questions.q: What does one Langevin dynamics step do?
questions.why: It climbs the log density and adds noise. With small steps and many iterations it samples from p.

questions.q: Why does annealed Langevin dynamics start at high noise?
options: The score is zero at low noise
At low noise the score is inaccurate in low-density regions; high noise smooths the distribution so the sampler can find all modes
High noise is faster to compute
questions.why: The sampler runs a few steps at each σ, moving from large to small, using the previous level's samples as starting points.

questions.q: In conditional flow matching with a straight path, what is the target velocity?
options: $x_1 - x_0$, the difference between the data sample and the noise sample
questions.why: With $x_t = (1-t)x_0 + t x_1$, the derivative is constant. The network regresses it at random t.

questions.q: What does a trained flow-matching model let you do at sampling time?
options: Sample by running the forward process
Integrate the learned velocity field from noise to data with an ODE solver
questions.why: Straighter paths need fewer integration steps, which is one appeal over curved diffusion trajectories.

questions.q: Why is conditioning on a single pair $(x_0, x_1)$ enough to learn the marginal velocity field?
options: The regression's minimiser is the conditional expectation of the per-pair velocity, which is the marginal field
It isn't; flow matching needs the full marginal
The model sees all pairs at once
Each pair has the same velocity
questions.why: This is the same argument that makes denoising score matching work without knowing the true score.

questions.q: How do diffusion and flow matching relate?
options: Diffusion sampling with a probability-flow ODE is a flow with a particular curved path; flow matching picks the path directly
questions.why: Both learn a time-dependent vector field. They differ in the interpolation path and in how the loss is weighted.

questions.q: The Fréchet distance between two Gaussians uses which formula?
questions.why: FID fits Gaussians to Inception features of real and generated images and computes this distance. Lower is better.

questions.q: Why is FID biased for small sample sizes?
options: Covariances estimated from few samples are noisy, which inflates the score
The formula only holds for 10,000 samples exactly
questions.why: Comparisons are only fair with the same number of samples, commonly 50,000.

questions.q: In a DiT, what does adaLN-Zero do?
options: Regresses scale, shift and gate values from the conditioning, with the gate initialised to zero so each block starts as identity
questions.why: The zero-initialised gate on each residual branch made training more stable than other conditioning schemes in the DiT paper.

questions.q: How does a DiT turn a latent image into tokens?
options: It flattens the whole image into one token
It uses one token per channel
It splits the latent into p×p patches and linearly embeds each one, adding positional embeddings
questions.why: Smaller patches give more tokens and better results at higher compute cost.

questions.q: Why do many modern diffusion models run in a VAE's latent space?
options: The latent is much smaller than pixel space, cutting compute while the decoder restores fine detail
The VAE removes the need for a noise schedule
questions.why: Latent diffusion moved most of the cost to an autoencoder trained once and reused.

questions.q: In a toy diffusion training step, which values are drawn at random?
options: A batch of data, a timestep per example and a noise tensor
questions.why: The model then predicts the noise from $x_t$ and t, and the loss is the mean squared error.

questions.q: A toy DDPM sampler starts from what?
options: $x_T \sim \mathcal N(0, I)$, then applies the reverse step from T down to 1
questions.why: Each step uses the model's prediction at the current t. The final $x_0$ is the sample.

questions.q: What does precision/recall for generative models measure that FID doesn't separate?
options: Sample quality (how many samples look real) separately from coverage (how much of the data distribution is produced)
questions.why: FID combines both in one number. A model can have good precision but poor recall, for example under strong guidance.
